newsitem.title: UK: Struggling gilts offer little cheer.
newsitem.headline: Struggling gilts offer little cheer.

text.p: British government bonds are likely to be bogged down by budget concerns, unfavourable economic data and Bank of England worries in coming weeks, analysts said on Wednesday.

And unless upcoming inflation data is spectacularly weak and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke comes up with a November budget to suit them, government bond or gilt investors have little to look forward to before the year ends. "The market is trading very heavily at the moment. There is just a feeling that the market wants to go down," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Investment Bank in London. "The BOE has made it clear at every opportunity in the last week or so that interest rates will have to rise further. That is really putting a cap on the market," he said.
Unemployment and earnings data relased on Wednesday underlined gilt investors' concerns analysts said.
The unemployment rate fell to 7.2 percent in October from 7.4 in September and unit wage costs rose an unexpectedly high 5.2 percent in the three months to September compared with a year ago.
"Gilts are under the strain of both political concerns and, more importantly, base rate concerns," said Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in London.

"We're facing an economy with an inflation impulse behind it, and while I don't think inflation is going to go up in the long term, the concerns are there and the Chancellor is going to address those concerns."

Forecasting that interest rates would rise again before a general election -- due by May 1997 -- Richardson said the recent underperformance of gilts, which bloated the 10-year gilt/Bund yield spread to 1.93 percent from around 1.55 in early October, was set to continue and could send the spread beyond two percent.

Minutes from the last monetary meeting between Chancellor Clarke and BOE Governor Eddie George showed George reiterating the need for base rates to rise above the currenct six percent level and expressing doubt that the government's 1997 inflation target of 2.5 percent would be met.

With the threat of further rate rises overhanging gilts, and sentiment favouring better-performing high-yielding debt markets such as Italy and Spain, Coleman too said gilts were unlikely to see rosier times in the short term.
Both Italian and Spanish bond markets have outperformed core European bonds dramatically in recent months, pushing past gilts on international spread trades.

Phil Tyson, European economist at HSBC Markets in London, said that against this background, international investors were very unlikely to be tempted into the gilt market -- even if it is now among the highest yielding markets in Europe.

Tyson said the the risk of another monetary tightening hitting the gilt market before general elections was now about 50/50, but said the 10-year spread to Bunds was still unlikely to increase beyond two percent.
"After today's (jobs and earnings) data there will obviously be mounting pressure from the Bank of England for a rate rise -- so the chances for one have certainly increased," he added.

Any bond-positive news along the way, such as softer than expected retail price numbers on Thursday or a fiscally responsible budget on November 26, could prompt some interim outperformance, he said, but that would be limited to spread convergence to around 1.65 percent.
